claims.claim: Evagrius Ponticus was a Christian monk and ascetic who lived from approximately 345 to 399 AD.
Evagrius was born in Ibora, Pontus, and was ordained as a reader by Basil the Great and later as a deacon by Gregory of Nazianzus.
Evagrius served as archdeacon in Constantinople and participated in the Second Ecumenical Council in 381.
Evagrius left Constantinople around 382, joined a monastic community in Jerusalem led by Rufinus and Melania the Elder, and took monastic vows in 383.
Evagrius spent the remainder of his life in Egypt, in the monastic communities of Nitria and Kellia, where he wrote extensively on asceticism.
Rerum monachalium rationes is a treatise in eleven sections describing the basic disciplines for living the monastic life.
The work's central concern is to cultivate hesychia—stillness or tranquility—and to advance the fight against evil powers.
The treatise offers advice on diet, dress, work, companionship, dwelling, visitation habits, wealth, possessions, commerce, fasting, vigils, and prayer.
Evagrius enjoins the constant contemplation of death, Hades and its torments, the day of judgment, punishments for the wicked, and rewards for the righteous as weapons against harmful thoughts.
The Greek title of the work is 'ΕΥΑΓΡΙΟΥ ΜΟΝΑΧΟΥ, ΤΩΝ ΚΑΤΑ ΜΟΝΑΧΩΝ ΠΡΑΓΜΑΤΩΝ ΤΑ ΑΙΤΙΑ, ΚΑΙ Η ΚΑΘ' ΗΣΥΧΙΑΝ ΤΟΥΤΩΝ ΠΑΡΑΘΕΣΙΣ', which identifies Evagrius as a monk.
The Latin title is 'EVAGRII MONACHI, Rerum monachalium rationes, earumque juxta quietem appositio'.
The work is also known as 'Hypotyposis' or 'Principles of the Monastic Life' or 'Foundations'.
